Tonight we have the pleasure of recognizing an outstanding student whose words have inspired many and captured the essence of civic engagement. Ms. Anya Sonosori, an ACPS eighth grade student from Henley Middle School, was named the grand prize winner of the UVA Equity Center's Voices of Democracy contest with her powerful and thought-provoking poem

"Democracy and Me." Last fall, the UVA Equity Center and the Krush Institute of Democracy invited 6th through 12th grade students from Charlottesville and Albemarle County to reflect on what democracy means in their lives. Anya's poem stood out among all submissions, offering a hopeful vision for the future, captured in these closing lines: So the future of democracy will be kindness and understanding, being considerate with ample planning,

because the future doesn't always have to be scary and mean. In the future of democracy, everyone will be seen. The Equity Center presented Henley Middle School with a copy of Anya's poem, underscoring the contest mission to ensure that all students voices are heard and that their perspectives on democracy are valued.

Teachers across our community use the contest prompts as a learning opportunity, encouraging students to explore the role of democracy in their daily lives. Even those who did not enter the competition found the exercise to be a meaningful and engaging classroom experience.

In addition to Anya's remarkable achievement, we are proud to recognize three other ACPS students who received honorable mention: Emerson Joy, or A.J. Wright, Jackson P. Burley Middle School, Grade 8; Halil Steny, Journey Middle School, Grade 8; and Max Harris, Western Albemarle High School, Grade 9.

This contest, along with the soon-to-open Karsh Institute of Democracy, serves as a reminder that civic engagement begins with young voices. Their reflections and aspirations for democracy challenge us all to envision a future that is inclusive, compassionate, and just. Please join me in congratulating Anya and our honorable mention recipients for their dedication to both writing and democracy.

Tonight I want to provide an update on where we stand with our instructional hours, how recent closures have impacted our bank time, and what steps we may need to take if more closures occur. Virginia state law requires school divisions to provide
990 instructional hours, or the equivalent of 180 school days each academic year. And if you're just looking at hours, each school day equates to six teaching hours.

If a district falls below this threshold, we have a few options to make up time, including adding instructional days to the calendar or extending the school day. At the start of the school year, we had 66 surplus instructional hours available.

However, after accounting for the flooding events in late September and early October, along with the two recent snow-related events, closures, we have used 55 of those hours, including six hours we regained by having a workday on January the 17th.

As of today, February the 13th, we have 11 banked hours remaining above the state mandated 990 hour requirement. Right now we have enough time to absorb one more full day closure without going below the required instructional hours.

However, if we have two or more additional closures, we will need to implement make up days to remain in compliance. If additional closures occur, we are prepared to adjust our calendar by converting the following non-instructional days into regular school days: Monday, April the 28th, we would convert from a professional development day to an instructional day.
Monday, March the 17th, convert from a professional development day to an instructional day. On Friday, March 28th, convert from a teacher work day to an instructional day.

If closures extend beyond the available makeup days, we may need to explore other options, including temporarily extending the length of the school day, extending the school year, applying for a waiver from the Virginia Board of Education in the event of a prolonged closure due to extreme weather.

At this point, we have some flexibility, but another two or more closures would require us to use designated make-up days. We will continue to monitor the situation closely and provide timely updates to our students, families, and staff.
